steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a reinforcement learning paper that generalizes KL regularization in policy optimization to Tsallis KL divergence and uses it to extend Munchausen Value Iteration. Motivate it from the practical problems of KL regularization, summarize what we do, and end with a short remark on related work about other divergences.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There is a lot of theoretical evidence that incorporating KL regularization into policy optimization in reinforcement learning is useful. The simplest approach is to regularize towards a uniform policy, which gives entropy regularization. It is more effective, however, to regularize towards the previous policy. If we choose KL regularization between policies that are updated consecutively, the optimal policy becomes a softmax over a uniform average of the full history of action value estimates. This averaging smooths out noise, and this allows better theoretical results.

Even with these theoretical benefits, using KL regularization in practice has some issues. The uniform average is well-known to be susceptible to outliers, and this issue is inherent to KL divergence. In practice people have widely implemented heuristics, such as assigning vanishing regularization coefficients to some of the estimates, to increase robustness and to accelerate learning. But for those heuristics the theoretical guarantees do not hold anymore. So a natural question is what alternatives to this KL divergence regularization we could consider, which let us overcome some of these disadvantages but still keep the benefits of restricting aggressive policy changes and smoothing errors.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
There is a lot of theoretical evidence that incorporating KL regularization into policy optimization in reinforcement learning is useful. The simplest approach is to regularize towards a uniform policy, which gives entropy regularization. It is more effective, however, to regularize towards the previous policy. If we choose KL regularization between policies that are updated consecutively, the optimal policy becomes a softmax over a uniform average of the full history of action value estimates. This averaging smooths out noise, and this allows better theoretical results.

Even with these theoretical benefits, using KL regularization in practice has some issues. The uniform average is well-known to be susceptible to outliers, and this issue is inherent to KL divergence. In practice people have widely implemented heuristics, such as assigning vanishing regularization coefficients to some of the estimates, to increase robustness and to accelerate learning. But for those heuristics the theoretical guarantees do not hold anymore. So a natural question is what alternatives to this KL divergence regularization we could consider, which let us overcome some of these disadvantages but still keep the benefits of restricting aggressive policy changes and smoothing errors.

In this work we explore one possible direction, which is generalizing to Tsallis KL divergences. Tsallis KL divergences were introduced for physics with a simple idea: the logarithm is replaced with the deformed q -logarithm. For policy optimization, though, the implication is that the resulting policy has quite a different form. Tsallis entropy with q=2 has actually been considered already for policy optimization, where Shannon entropy is replaced with Tsallis entropy in order to maintain stochasticity in the policy. These policies are called sparsemax policies, because they put the probability on the higher-valued actions and truncate the probability to zero for the lower-valued actions. Intuitively this should have the benefit of keeping stochasticity but only among the most promising actions, which is unlike the Boltzmann policy that keeps nonzero probability on all actions. Unfortunately using Tsallis entropy alone did not give significant benefits, and it often performed worse than existing methods. What we find, however, is that using a Tsallis KL divergence to the previous policy does give notable gains.

First we show how Tsallis KL regularization can be incorporated into the standard value iteration updates, and we prove that convergence is maintained under this generalization from KL regularization to Tsallis KL regularization. Then we characterize what types of policies are learned under Tsallis KL, and we highlight that the relationship to past action-values is now more complex than a simple uniform average. Then we show how to extend Munchausen Value Iteration (MVI) to use Tsallis KL regularization, and we call this MVI(q). The naming is meant to highlight that this strictly generalizes MVI: setting q=1 recovers MVI exactly. Finally we compare MVI(q=2) with MVI (the standard choice, where q=1), and we get significant performance improvements in Atari.

Remark: There is a growing body of literature that studies generalizations of KL divergence in RL. Prior work discussed the inherent drawback of KL divergence in generative modeling and proposed using \beta - and \gamma -divergence to allow a weighted average of sample contribution. These divergences belong to the category known as the f -divergence, which is commonly used in other machine learning domains, including generative modeling and imitation learning. In RL, other work discussed using tail adaptive f -divergence to enforce the mass-covering property, and another work discussed using \alpha -divergence. Tsallis KL divergence, however, has not been studied in RL yet.

steps.text:

This averaging smooths out noise, and this allows better theoretical results [2,3,1,4].

Even with these theoretical benefits, using KL regularization in practice has some issues. The uniform average is well-known to be susceptible to outliers, and this issue is inherent to KL divergence [5]. In practice people have widely implemented heuristics, such as assigning vanishing regularization coefficients to some of the estimates, to increase robustness and to accelerate learning [6,7,8]. But for those heuristics the theoretical guarantees do not hold anymore [1,4]. For policy optimization, though, the implication is that the resulting policy has quite a different form. Tsallis entropy with q=2 has actually been considered already for policy optimization [11,12], where Shannon entropy is replaced with Tsallis entropy in order to maintain stochasticity in the policy. These policies are called sparsemax policies, because they put the probability on the higher-valued actions and truncate the probability to zero for the lower-valued actions. Intuitively this should have the benefit of keeping stochasticity but only among the most promising actions, which is unlike the Boltzmann policy that keeps nonzero probability on all actions. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
There is ample theoretical evidence that incorporating KL regularization into policy optimization in reinforcement learning is useful. The most basic approach is to regularize towards a uniform policy, which results in entropy regularization. More effective, however, is to regularize towards the previous policy. By choosing KL regularization between consecutively updated policies, the optimal policy becomes a softmax over a uniform average of the full history of action value estimates [1]. This averaging smooths out noise, which allows for better theoretical results [2,3,1,4].

Despite these theoretical benefits, there are some issues with using KL regularization in practice. It is well-known that the uniform average is susceptible to outliers; this issue is inherent to KL divergence [5]. In practice, heuristics such as assigning vanishing regularization coefficients to some estimates have been widely implemented to increase robustness and accelerate learning [6,7,8]. However, the theoretical guarantees no longer hold for those heuristics [1,4]. A natural question is what alternatives to this KL divergence regularization we can consider, that allow us to overcome some of these disadvantages while keeping the benefits of restricting aggressive policy changes and smoothing errors.

In this work, we explore one possible direction by generalizing to Tsallis KL divergences. Tsallis KL divergences were introduced for physics [9,10] using a simple idea: replacing the logarithm with the deformed q -logarithm. For policy optimization, however, the implication is that we get quite a different form for the resulting policy. Tsallis entropy with q=2 has in fact already been considered for policy optimization [11,12], by replacing Shannon entropy with Tsallis entropy to maintain stochasticity in the policy. The resulting policies are called sparsemax policies, because they concentrate the probability on higher-valued actions and truncate the probability to zero for lower-valued actions. Intuitively, this should have the benefit of maintaining stochasticity, but only amongst the most promising actions, unlike the Boltzmann policy, which keeps nonzero probability on all actions. Unfortunately, using only Tsallis entropy did not provide significant benefits, and often performed worse than existing methods. We find, however, that using a Tsallis KL divergence to the previous policy does provide notable gains.

We first show how to incorporate Tsallis KL regularization into the standard value iteration updates, and prove that convergence is maintained under this generalization from KL regularization to Tsallis KL regularization. We then characterize the types of policies learned under Tsallis KL, highlighting that there is now a more complex relationship to past action-values than a simple uniform average. Next we show how to extend Munchausen Value Iteration (MVI) [13] to use Tsallis KL regularization, which we call MVI(q). This naming highlights that it is a strict generalization of MVI: by setting q=1, we exactly recover MVI. Finally, we compare MVI(q=2) with MVI (the standard choice where q=1), and obtain significant performance improvements in Atari.

Remark: There is a growing body of literature that studies generalizations of KL divergence in RL [14,15]. [5] discussed the inherent drawback of KL divergence in generative modeling and proposed using \beta - and \gamma -divergence to allow for a weighted average of sample contribution. These divergences fall under the category known as the f -divergence [16], which is commonly used in other machine learning domains, including generative modeling [17,18,19] and imitation learning [20,21]. In RL, [22] discussed using tail adaptive f -divergence to enforce the mass-covering property, and [23] discussed the use of \alpha -divergence. Tsallis KL divergence, however, has not yet been studied in RL.
